text: Dolphins and Language Learning
A

No single trait has been linked more closely with the human species than language. However, the definition of language and its uniqueness as a human trait continue to be studied and debated. Some scholars, such as the linguist Noam Chomsky, take the view that language is an adaptation supported by specialist modifications of the brain that appear only in humans. Others, such as the anthropologist Barbara King, favor a continuity position, which suggests that language must have its roots in early human forms of communication, and that some of these may still exist in modern animal species.

text: B

Dolphins produce various types of sounds, including clicks, burst- pulse emissions, and whistles. Clicks are used for echolocation – the dolphin's form of sonar – which allows the dolphin to examine its world by listening to the echoes returning from objects struck by the clicks. Sounds such as whistling may indicate the dolphin's psychological state, ranging from pleasure to anger. However, much remains to be learned about these types of vocalizations. For example, it is unclear whether these whistles are intentionally used for communication.

text: C

During the 1960s, researchers attempted to understand whether the whistle vocalizations might be a form of language. Investigators recorded whistles from many dolphins in many different situations, but soon realized the vocalizations were not complicated enough to support anything approaching a human language system. Some of the early work instead pointed to the stereotype of the whistles from individual dolphins, which led researchers David and Melba Caldwell to suggest that the whistle functioned principally as a 'signature', with each individual dolphin producing a distinctive signature. Presumably, this enabled that individual to be identified by others.

text: D

Other researchers have noted, however, that the whistle involves a great deal of flexibility. Scientists at the Kewalo Basin Marine Mammal Laboratory at the University of Hawaii reported a study showing that a dolphin could use its whistle mode to imitate a variety of sounds that were generated by a computer and then broadcast underwater in the dolphin's habitat. After further research, Peter Tyack reported that one dolphin could reproduce another's whistle, thereby possibly referring to or calling that individual. The ability to do this is recognized as a basic characteristic of language. However, we still do not know to what extent the dolphin's whistles may be used to refer to things other than themselves or another dolphin.

text: E

From the mid-1950s to the mid-1960s, researcher John Lilly promoted the idea that bottlenose dolphins might possess an innate language. He based his supposition on this species' exceptionally large brain. He reasoned that this must be a powerful information processor having capabilities for advanced levels of intellectual accomplishment, including the development of a language. He set about to uncover the supposed language. Failing in that quest, he then attempted, also ineffectively, to get the dolphins which he kept in his laboratories to understand human vocal language – English in this case.

text: F

The Kewalo Basin dolphin language studies of the mid-1970s, which were begun by Louis Herman and colleagues, emphasized language comprehension from the start. The researchers, working principally with a bottlenose dolphin named Akeakamai, constructed a sign language in which the gestures of a person's arms and hands corresponded to words. The words referred to objects from Akeakamai's habitat, and what the dolphin could do with them. There were also words such as 'left' and 'right', which described the position of the objects with respect to the dolphin, and enabled it to identify a specific object, e.g. left hoop versus right hoop. The vocabulary of some 30 to 40 words, together with word- order rules, allowed for many thousands of unique sentences to be constructed, the simplest being instructions to the dolphin to perform named actions to named objects. In one experiment conducted by Herman's team, a sequence of two gestures, which roughly meant 'surfboard over', directed the dolphin to leap over the surfboard. More complex sentences required the dolphin to construct a relationship between two objects, such as taking one named object to another named object. To interpret the relational sentences correctly, the dolphin had to take account of both word meaning and word order.

text: G

The results showed that Akeakamai was capable of interpreting these various types of sentences correctly, as evidenced by her ability to carry out the required instructions. These were the first published results showing convincingly an animal's ability to process both semantic (relating to the meaning of language) and syntactic (relating to word order in sentences) information in interpreting language- like instructions. This ability is considered a core attribute of any human language.

text: H

Dolphins have been tested in many formal procedures, leading to a fuller understanding of their competencies. In general, high levels of parental care and high degrees of brain activity go together. It is easy to see how the extensive development of the brain in dolphins, and the resulting cognitive skills of some members of this group, have derived from the demands of survival in the dolphin community. These challenges include both co- operation and competition among peers, particularly important because of the prolonged development of the young.
